```{r setup-child, child = "helpers/_setup.Rmd"}
```

```{r}
#| label: library
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
library(housepi)
housepi_theme_set()
set.seed(42)
```

Here we present all available options for the choice of the prior and Monte Carlo proposal in housepi.

# Continuous priors

To perform the sampling we consider the "test" model, i.e. a data independent template model, with log-likelihood always equal to zero.
Here's the full list of available continuous distributions present in housepi:
```{r}
#| label: continuous-priors-density
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots for prior distributions available in housepi for Bayesian inference: uniform, normal, lognormal, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh, beta and exponential.
#|  Each panel displays the estimated probability density function in blue obtained from MCMC sampling.
# create an instance of the model 'test'
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  # continuous distributions in housepi
  add_parameter(
    uniform = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0, max = 1),
    normal = list(prior = "normal", mean = 0, sd = 1),
    lognormal = list(prior = "lognormal", meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1),
    gamma = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),
    weibull = list(prior = "weibull", shape = 2, scale = 1),
    rayleigh = list(prior = "rayleigh", scale = 1),
    beta = list(prior = "beta", shape1 = 2, shape2 = 1),
    exponential = list(prior = "exponential", rate = 1)
  ) |>
  # perform the sampling with the inference command
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens()
```

Here we associated definitions of parameters with default proposals and custom arguments.
Argument defaults match the base R sampling functions: `normal` starts from `mean = 0` and `sd = 1` as in `rnorm()`, `exponential` from `rate = 1` as in `rexp()`.
Arguments carrying no default in base R, such as the gamma `shape`, stay required here too.

# Provide a custom domain

Here we test various examples to show how to select a custom domain for the variables.
This will automatically impose a truncation of the prior of the parameter.
We do this with the arguments `min` (minimum) and `max` (maximum).

```{r}
#| label: truncation-demo
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four density plots demonstrating truncation options for normal distribution.
#|  Orange dashed lines indicate truncation boundaries applied to distributions.
library(ggplot2)

new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    default = list(prior = "normal"),
    below = list(prior = "normal", min = -1),
    above = list(prior = "normal", max = 1),
    both = list(prior = "normal", min = -1, max = 1)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(0, 0.65)) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(Parameter = c("below", "above", "both", "both"),
                               xintercept = c(-1, 1, -1, 1)),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept),
             linetype = 2)
```

# Provide a location parameter

All functions and distributions in housepi allow for a location parameter `loc` to translate the support of the distribution:

```{r}
#| label: location-parameter-demo
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots showing gamma distributions with different location parameters.
#|  Four panels display gamma distributions with location parameters set to 0, 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
#|  Vertical dashed lines indicate the minimum of each shifted support.
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    gamma_0 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),
    gamma_1 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1, loc = 1),
    gamma_2 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1, loc = 2),
    gamma_3 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1, loc = 3)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10)) +
  geom_vline(
    data = data.frame(Parameter = c("gamma_0", "gamma_1", "gamma_2", "gamma_3"),
                      xintercept = c(0, 1, 2, 3)),
    aes(xintercept = xintercept),
    linetype = 2)
```

# Discrete priors

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-discrete
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

Here's the full list of available discrete distributions present in housepi:

```{r}
#| label: discrete-priors-hist
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Five histograms displaying discrete prior distributions available in housepi: poisson, binomial, negative binomial, geometric, and categorical.
#|  Orange bars represent probability mass functions for integer-valued outcomes obtained from MCMC sampling.

# discrete distributions in housepi
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    poisson = list(prior = "poisson", lambda = 2),
    binomial = list(prior = "binomial", size = 4, prob = 0.5),
    negative_binomial = list(prior = "negative_binomial", size = 4, prob = 0.5),
    geometric = list(prior = "geometric", prob = 0.5),
    categorical = list(prior = "categorical", low = 0.3, mid = 0.1, high = 0.6)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(binwidth = 1)
```

# Discretize continuous priors

Previous continuous priors can be chosen to be discretized using the argument `discr`.

```{r}
#| label: discretized-priors-hist
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Seven histograms showing discretized versions of continuous prior distributions: uniform, normal, lognormal, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh, and exponential.

new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    uniform = list(prior = "uniform", discr = TRUE),
    normal = list(prior = "normal", discr = TRUE),
    lognormal = list(prior = "lognormal", discr = TRUE),
    gamma = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, discr = TRUE),
    weibull = list(prior = "weibull", shape = 2, discr = TRUE),
    rayleigh = list(prior = "rayleigh", discr = TRUE),
    exponential = list(prior = "exponential", discr = TRUE)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(binwidth = 1)
```

Note that here we dropped all arguments that allow for default values.

# Discretization in practice

Depending on the distribution support, the discretization is defined as:

* Left discretization: average probability between the closest lower and larger integer;
* Center discretization: average probability over a symmetric interval of width 1 centered at the integer (i.e. between integer − 0.5 and integer + 0.5).

With this scheme normalization is respected, however the shape of the distribution might not be the expected one.
You can use the function `browse_distributions` to return a Distribution object from housepi and explore its methods.

```{r}
#| label: discretization-scheme-plot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Histogram illustrating the discretization scheme as average probability.
gamma_cont <- browse_distributions("gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1)
gamma_discr <- browse_distributions("gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1, discr = TRUE)

ggplot(dplyr::tibble(x = seq(0, 9, 1), y = gamma_discr$pdf(x),
                     z1 = gamma_cont$cdf(x + 1), z0 = gamma_cont$cdf(x))) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin  = x, xmax  = x + 1,
                ymin  = 0, ymax  = z1 - z0, fill  = "average_prob"),
            color = "coral") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y, color = "discretised")) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x, xend = x + 1, y = y, yend = y), color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(average_prob = "orange"),
                    labels = c(average_prob = "average probability")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(discretised = "black"),
                     labels = c(discretised = "discretised"))
```

# Monte Carlo proposals

MCMC proposals determine how candidate parameter values are drawn at each step.
They come in two families.

*Independence samplers* draw a fresh value from a distribution, like the variable's own:

* **forward**: direct sampling from the variable's own defining distribution;
* a **distribution name** (e.g. `"normal"`): sampling from that distribution,
  with its parameters supplied as `proposal_mean`, `proposal_sd`, ...

*Random walks* perturb the current value:

* **rw**: Gaussian increments;
* **rw_log**: multiplicative log-normal increments (not appropriate for negative
  nor discrete values);
* **rw_unif**: uniform (bounded) increments inside a window.

Only the random walks are adaptable.
By default, housepi tunes the scale on the fly to target an acceptance rate of 44% [@roberts_weak_1997].
This is enabled by supplying `adapt = N` to `run_inference()`.
Here `N` is the number of adaptation iterations run before the MCMC `steps`.
The adaptation uses a Robbins-Monro update at every iteration
on an acceptance rate estimated with exponentially weighted moving average.
The scale is initialized from the prior's interquartile range.

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-proposals
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "brightblue")
```

```{r}
#| label: adaptation-trace
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four trace plots comparing the same MCMC proposal mechanisms with
#|  proposal_scale left adaptive.  All chains mix well after a short adaptation phase.

new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    forward = list(prior = "normal", min = 0, proposal = "forward"),
    rw_unif = list(prior = "normal", min = 0, proposal = "rw_unif"),
    rw = list(prior = "normal", min = 0, proposal = "rw"),
    rw_log = list(prior = "normal", min = 0, proposal = "rw_log")
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

Already with the default adaptive steps, mixing is good across the random-walk
proposals — at the cost of the additional steps before sampling.

## Fix proposal scales

The scale of the proposals can be fixed by supplying an explicit `proposal_scale`.
This pins the scale to the chosen value and disables adaptation for that variable.

```{r}
#| label: proposals-trace
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four trace plots comparing MCMC proposal mechanisms with a deliberately
#|  oversized pinned scale.  Sampling shows poor mixing for all parametric
#|  mechanisms.
# select an extremely large proposal scale 'sigma'
sigma <- 100
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    forward = list(prior = "normal", min = 0, proposal = "forward"),
    rw_unif = list(prior = "normal", min = 0,
                   proposal = "rw_unif", proposal_scale = !!sigma),
    rw = list(prior = "normal", min = 0,
              proposal = "rw", proposal_scale = !!sigma),
    rw_log = list(prior = "normal", min = 0,
                  proposal = "rw_log", proposal_scale = !!sigma)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

Warnings and trace plots show bad mixing:
the over-sized scale made the random-walk proposals barely move.
On the contrary, the `forward` mechanism mixes as usual.
Handle `proposal_scale` with care!
